title: AuroraPay - POC scoping: workload modeling
summary: POC scoping focused on workload characterization and traffic modeling for AuroraPay's conversational payments assistant. Discussed QPS/concurrency targets, token distributions, acceptable latencies, benchmark plan, security/hosting preferences (Dedicated vs Private/VPC), and success criteria for go/no-go. Agreed next steps: share benchmark template, run initial load tests next week, schedule security review with infra team.
next_steps: Redwood to send benchmark template + example request trace (Maya) by 2026-02-19
Customer to provide 7 days worth of anonymized request logs or a sampling (Ravi) by 2026-02-24
Schedule Dedicated vs Private security call (Rowan to propose times) by 2026-02-20
Plan load test window (2 hours) week of 2026-02-23 (Diego to run)
action_items: Maya - send benchmark spreadsheet + sample postman collection - due 2026-02-19
Ravi - export anonymized request traces (1 week) or produce synthetic traffic profile - due 2026-02-24
Diego - prepare test harness and initial model selection suggestions (quantized variants) - due 2026-02-21
Rowan - coordinate security review invite and attach SOC2 docs - due 2026-02-20
transcript:
[00:00:03] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya with Redwood Inference, this is Diego our solutions engineer, and Rowan from CS. Can you hear us ok?
[00:00:10] Lena (AuroraPay CTO): Yes, loud and clear. Thanks for making time.
[00:00:14] Ravi (SRE): Hey. Quick heads up, Sara couldn't make the first 10 min but she'll join in.
[00:00:20] Diego (Redwood SE): No problem. Today we're aiming to map out the POC success criteria and get a concrete workload model — QPS, concurrency, token distribution, that kind of thing.
[00:00:31] Tom (Head of Payments): High level, we want the assistant to handle payment flows, auth prompts, and some multi-step clarifications. Latency matters, but accuracy and data isolation are top priorities.
[00:00:45] Maya: Great. Can you run through current usage and what you expect during peak?
[00:00:50] Lena: Right now our live chat had about 300 unique interactions per hour during daytime and spikes to maybe 1,200 an hour during promos. But for the assistant we think Q1 launch might see 5 to 10 QPS peak as customers adopt, longer term 20 QPS peak sounds possible.
[00:01:08] Ravi: To add, concurrency per user is low — most sessions are single-turn but some flows can spawn multi-turn up to 6 messages. So concurrency of requests hitting the model concurrently is around 8–12 for peak.
[00:01:23] Diego: So you're thinking average QPS of ~4–6 with bursts to 20, and concurrency up to 12. That's helpful. For planning we usually ask for a 95th percentile target and typical token sizes.
[00:01:35] Sara (ML Eng, joined): Sorry for the delay, I'm here.
[00:01:39] Maya: No worries. Could you walk us through token distributions — prompt length vs response length, and any system-level context you include?
[00:01:46] Sara: Sure. Most user prompts are short — 10–40 tokens when simple questions; payment requests with context (transaction history snippet) can be 150–300 tokens. We expect the assistant to generate anywhere from 40 tokens up to 400 for receipts or explanation — average output around 120 tokens. Our system injects a 200 token context for user metadata and policy rules on every request.
[00:02:10] Diego: So end-to-end request tokens total could be prompt 100–500 plus output 40–400, with an embedded static system context ~200. For sizing, we usually look at total input + output tokens per request and distribution. That matches a heavy tail distribution.
[00:02:25] Ravi: Yes heavy tail, during promos there are many short ones but we do have long form responses occasionally.
[00:02:31] Maya: For SLOs, what's acceptable? 95th percentile latency we're targeting?
[00:02:36] Tom: We want interactive feel — under 500ms for simple confirmations is ideal but we know longer completions might be slower. If 95p for a 256-token generation is under 800ms that's acceptable.
[00:02:48] Diego: Understood. For a POC we'll target 95th < 800ms for up to 256 token responses. We'll run benchmarks to measure P50/P95/P99 and cost per 1k tokens.
[00:02:58] Lena: We also need to validate data handling: encryption at rest, KMS integration, and audit logs. We'll likely need Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC peering.
[00:03:10] Rowan: We'll send our SOC2 pack and private deployment checklist. For the POC do you want us to run on Redwood Hosted first or do you require Dedicated?
[00:03:19] Ravi: For initial perf tests hosted is fine as long as data in transit is encrypted; but for any production-like PII tests we need Dedicated or Private.
[00:03:28] Maya: Okay, typical approach: start on Hosted to validate baseline model/latency, then move to Dedicated capacity for representative perf and VPC testing. We'll note that in the plan.
[00:03:37] Diego: Now, on modeling the traffic for load tests: we'll need a representative sample of request traces (timestamps, token counts, success/failure flags). If you can't share real traces, a synthetic distribution works — we can provide a generator.
[00:03:49] Ravi: We can export logs with PII redacted; team can do that.
[00:03:53] Sara: Also note we run a lot of short embedding requests for search indexing, different workload than chat. Might want a separate benchmark for embeddings throughput.
[00:04:03] Diego: Good point. For embeddings we size on throughput (requests/sec) and vector store write QPS; typical vector dims 1k? how big are vectors?
[00:04:09] Sara: We use 1,024 dim vectors for one job, but for user session search we use 384 dim models. Those are lower cost — we'll include both.
[00:04:17] Maya: Let's capture two workload profiles: 1) Conversation assistant (chat gen) — mixed token sizes, bursty; 2) Embedding pipeline — steady high throughput, smaller responses.
[00:04:26] Tom: Timeline — we'd like to have a POC result in 3 weeks. Week 1 gather data and config, Week 2 run benchmarks and iterate, Week 3 validation and security review. Is that realistic?
[00:04:36] Diego: It's tight but doable if we get traces this week. Benchmarks typically take a few days to run for different model variants and quantization profiles.
[00:04:45] Lena: Success criteria: functional parity on major flows, 95p latency under 800ms for 256 tokens for chat, embedding throughput of >= 100 QPS for 384-dim vectors with 99p error rate under 1%. Also clear path for data isolation.
[00:04:59] Maya: I'll write those down — functional parity, 95p latency <800ms (256 tokens), embedding throughput >=100 QPS for 384-dim, and clear documentation/auditability for data. Anything to add?
[00:05:09] Ravi: Cost estimates matter to us too — we want unit cost per 1k tokens and projected monthly cost at 20 QPS steady for planning.
[00:05:16] Diego: We'll produce a cost model (tokens, GPU hours, P99 tail) in the spreadsheet. We'll include recommendations for batching, KV cache use, and quantization to reduce units.
[00:05:26] Sara: For quantization we prefer 4-bit if accuracy loss is small — we can test LLM variants.
[00:05:30] Maya: Ok next, benchmarks specifics: we'll run these scenarios — cold start single request latency, steady-state 1 minute at avg QPS, spike test to peak QPS for 10 minutes, and a 2-hour soak at expected peak to look for memory growth.
[00:05:45] Diego: Yep and we'll collect P50/P95/P99 latencies, token throughput, GPU util, and per-request memory/KV cache hit rates. Also the cost per token and tail latency percentiles.
[00:05:58] Lena: For environment can you simulate our payloads? We have a couple of templates — payment confirm, auth challenge, transaction history with PCI redaction.
[00:06:06] Diego: If you share anonymized traces we'll mimic exact token lengths and distributions. Otherwise, we provide a synthetic generator tuned to your reported distribution.
[00:06:14] Tom: On model selection, do you have recommended families? We care about latency and cost.
[00:06:20] Diego: For latency-sensitive short responses, smaller Llama-like or optimized Mistral variants work well. For richer long completions, a medium LLM with KV cache benefits is better. We'll recommend a shortlist after we see token sizes. Also consider quantized 4-bit checkpoints on Dedicated to save cost.
[00:06:35] Sara: Can you run tests with both hosted and dedicated to compare network and peering impacts?
[00:06:39] Maya: Yes, we'll run both where possible. Note that hosted will include our normal networking path so latencies may be slightly higher than a VPC with peering.
[00:06:47] Ravi: Security — we need KMS, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and audit logs. Also need proof that logs don't store full PII.
[00:06:55] Rowan: We'll attach the SOC2 report and a short FAQ about data residency and retention.
[00:06:59] Lena: Great. Can we get a rough schedule now?
[00:07:03] Maya: Week plan:
- Mon/Tue (this week): gather traces and pick initial model candidates
- Wed: Redwood sends benchmark template and cost model
- Thu/Fri: Diego runs initial 1-hour benchmark on hosted and shares results
- Following week: run Dedicated tests and 2-hour soak, do embedding throughput test
- Security review scheduled mid second week
[00:07:25] Tom: Sounds reasonable.
[00:07:28] Ravi: One operational detail — our traffic is regionally split NA/EU 70/30; can you pin region for dedicated nodes?
[00:07:35] Maya: Yes, Dedicated can be region pinned. We'll document routing and fallback policies.
[00:07:40] Diego: For traffic modeling we'll assume a 70/30 split and ensure tests include EU latency constraints.
[00:07:46] Sara: Also want to see cost tradeoffs for caching TTLs — a small prefix cache could dramatically reduce token counts for repetitive prompts.
[00:07:54] Diego: We'll model cache hit rate scenarios (0%, 30%, 60%) and show cost/latency impact.
[00:07:59] Maya: Any blockers to start?
[00:08:02] Lena: We need the benchmark template and a non-PII export. Otherwise no blockers.
[00:08:06] Maya: We'll get that to you today. Diego, you'll own the test runs?
[00:08:10] Diego: Yep. I'll prepare a harness and send the plan.
[00:08:13] Rowan: I'll coordinate security docs and send calendar invites for the review.
[00:08:18] Tom: Ok wrap up: we expect deliverables — benchmark spreadsheet, initial hosted run results, Dedicated run plan, security pack.
[00:08:26] Maya: I'll recap in a follow-up email and attach the template.
[00:08:29] Ravi: Thanks everyone.
[00:08:31] Lena: Thanks.
[00:08:33] Maya: End call.

[00:18:00] *automated note: meeting continued off-record for 10 minutes with informal chat about integration teams*
[00:30:12] *transcription glitch: "KV cass" should be KV cache; "Redwood Dedicate" should be Redwood Dedicated*

Notes on the traffic model we discussed: average QPS target 4–6, peak bursts to 20 QPS, concurrency 8–12. Token distributions: typical request (including system context) 200–600 input tokens, expected output 40–400 tokens, average total tokens per request ~320. Embeddings: 384-dim throughput target >=100 QPS, 1024-dim background batch runs. Success criteria spelled out in next steps above.

References shared: benchmark template link (to be sent), SOC2 pack (Rowan will attach), sample synthetic traffic generator (Redwood repo link to be provided).
